rationale: B wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and turns every angle into a reporter's next question. "Sweetgreen says its robot-assembled stores run higher margins than human-run ones" is a little blunt, but the proof list asks for margin definition, capex, throughput, and sample size. A has useful bones, but "The $15 salad" and "premium fast-casual needs human hands" smuggle in assumptions the update never gave us. That is not color; that is how a reporter finds the loose thread.
gaps_in_A: "The $15 salad" is invented. The update gives no price point, and a cute headline is not a fact.
"premium, customizable, ingredient-forward" and "the tier where automation couldn't go" are unsupported category claims. Interesting thesis, wrong burden of proof.
"ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage" is a generic backdrop, not a supplied peg. It makes the labor angle sound more current than the facts allow.
The next step points to "meanest-editor" when the real next move is proof-gathering and journalist fit: margin range, staffing numbers, and source names.
gaps_in_B: "human-run ones" is slightly sloppy. The fact pattern says traditional stores, not necessarily all-human operations.
The first two angles are close cousins: "store-level margins" and "path to profit runs through automation" could collapse into one business/equities pitch unless the outlet split is enforced.
"Is there any current news peg here? None was supplied" undercuts the set too much. The expansion plus margin disclosure is a current company-news peg; what is missing is an external newsjack peg.
It leaves the broader fast-casual operations/category angle on the table, though that omission is better than inventing a fake one.
